Every token says ERC-20 on the label.

That is supposed to mean they all work the same way, so apps can treat them the same. I opened up 4,740 tokens on 6 chains, including the 4,198 biggest by market cap, and tested what they actually do. Then I simulated buying and selling 27,090 brand-new ones an hour after launch. They don’t work the same.

Built with a swarm of AI agents, so there will be mistakes. Every number links to its evidence. Corrections welcome.

Start reading Explore the data

What is in the 4,740?

The top 2,000 tokens by market cap on Ethereum, the top 500 on each of BNB Chain, Base, Arbitrum and Polygon, and the 198 ranked on Optimism. On top of that, tokens on Uniswap’s default list and tokens with high DEX volume.

This has cost real money.

Apps are written on the assumption that a token behaves like any other. Twice in 2020 it didn’t.

So what do the biggest tokens actually do? Start with the biggest stablecoin.

Part one: the biggest tokens

What the biggest tokens actually do

Things the standard does not promise. Each one can break an app or surprise a holder.

USDT’s transfer() says nothing back.

The standard says transfer() should answer true when it works. USDT on Ethereum answers nothing.

What breaks An app written by the book rejects every USDT transfer on Ethereum. It is rare, with 15 of 4,170 measured top tokens doing it, but the biggest stablecoin is one of them.

That is why DeFi code wraps token calls in helpers like SafeERC20 from OpenZeppelin.

Some tokens fail the other way. When a transfer cannot happen, LDO on Ethereum answers false instead of reverting, so an app that never reads the answer carries on as if the money moved returns false when balance or allowance falls short(saved call). 24 of 4,175 measured tokens do this.

What the standard says

› transfer(to, amount)

‹ true

What USDT on Ethereum does

› transfer(to, amount)

‹ (nothing)

An app written to the standardrequire(transfer(to, amount) == true)

That is what a token says back. What it counts in can differ too.

Same name, a trillion apart.

Tokens store amounts as whole numbers. The decimals setting says where the decimal point goes. USDT on Ethereum has 6 decimals. Binance-Peg USDT on BNB Chain has 18.

What breaks Carry the same number over without converting and the amount is off by a factor of a trillion.

Even with the right decimals, the amount you sent is not always the amount that arrives.

Some tokens quietly take a cut.

29 of 4,066 measured top tokens (0.7%) charge a fee on transfer, so less arrives than you sent. That is the kind of mismatch behind the Balancer drain.

Others change your balance with no transfer at all. 26 of 2,484 drifted on their own during a week of watching.

What breaks An app that books the amount it sent holds less than it recorded. An app that saves a balance finds a different number later.

And some rules nobody wrote down at all.

Then the small rules.

Code that has never met one finds out the hard way. A payout batch with one zero amount in it, sent in BNB on Ethereum, fails as a whole.

  • 138of 4,078 measured

    tokens refuse a transfer of zero. BNB on Ethereum is one of them transfer reverted(saved call).

    An app that sends a zero amount, to batch a payout for example, gets a revert for the whole batch.

  • 35of 4,070 measured

    tokens stop at about 79 billion whole tokens (296 base units at 18 decimals). UNI, COMP and ONDO are among them.

    Send more and the transfer reverts. Approve “unlimited” and you get a cap instead. UNI: capped at the uint96 maximum(saved call).

  • USDT

    on Ethereum makes you reset an approval to zero before changing it must reset approval to zero first(saved call).

    An app that raises an allowance in one step gets a revert.

  • WETH

    lets an owner move its own tokens with no approval at all can spend its own tokens without approval(saved call).

    An app that treats an approval as the gate for moving tokens finds no gate for the owner.

  • DACITY

    on Base shows a balance for an address that has never been used a never-used address shows a balance(saved call).

    An app that treats a nonzero balance as a real, funded user is fooled.

All of that is about one chain at a time. The same ticker on another chain can be a different token.

Same ticker, different token.

Remember USDT and its decimals: one coin, a trillion apart on two chains. That is not a one-off. The same ticker on another chain is usually a separate contract, deployed by someone else, with its own rules. What a token does on one chain tells you little about the same ticker elsewhere.

PayPal’s PYUSD shows it. I simulated sending each copy a transfer to the Tornado Cash router, an address the US sanctions authority delisted on 2025-03-21. On Ethereum and Arbitrum the token refuses. On Polygon it lets the transfer through. It is not in our tested set on the other three chains.

Why? The test sends to the same router address on every chain, so a refusal means that copy keeps its own list with the address on it. What the data does show is that the copies run 3 different pieces of code. Polygon’s is a small 855-byte shell that 3 tokens in our set use, PYUSD one of them, so it was built differently from the other two. A refusal can also come from a list nobody updated after the delisting. Exactly why Polygon’s copy lets the transfer through, I do not know.

What breaks An app that assumes one chain’s behaviour carries over to another gets it wrong in either direction.

UNI’s quirk never left Ethereum.

Earlier, UNI on Ethereum capped an “unlimited” approval. On the other four chains it does not. The copies are again different code, and here the data says a bit more. On Arbitrum, UNI runs one 760-byte contract shared by 225 tokens in our set, UNI and LINK among them. On Polygon it is another shared contract, 2,949 bytes.

A template shared by many unrelated tokens is what bridge-issued tokens tend to look like, and it would explain why they carry none of the original’s quirks. On Polygon our data marks UNI as a bridged copy, along with 146 of the 163 other tokens that share its code. On Arbitrum the pattern looks the same, but I have not traced those copies to a bridge.

What breaks Testing the Ethereum token and assuming the rest match, or the other way round.

  • Polygon2,949 bytes of code, the same code as 164 tokens hereno cap
  • Optimism3,890 bytes of code, the same code as 10 tokens hereno cap

It is not just two tokens.

The old quirks of the standard live on Ethereum. All 15 top tokens whose transfer() says nothing back are Ethereum tokens. Among the top five hundred on the other five chains, it is 0 of 2,181.

Individual tokens scatter the same way. USDe, LINK and WBTC each answer differently from chain to chain. There is no chain you can test and then assume for the rest.

Someone decides which of those lists and switches exist. Who holds them?

Then the switches someone else holds.

Some tokens ship with a pause button or a freeze list, and you are not the one holding it. Tokenized stocks and funds are the extreme case: 474 of the 510 among the top tokens have a blocklist.

BUIDL, a tokenized fund, goes further: it rejects transfers to wallets it has not approved rejected: permission required(saved call). PEPE still has a blocklist in its code, but its owner gave up the role renounced(saved call). Whether anyone can still use the list, the code alone does not say.

What breaks A paused token fails every transfer. A blocked address keeps its balance but can’t send it.

26.2%

can be paused. One call and nobody can move them.

1,097 of 4,183 ranked tokens measured

22.0%

can block specific addresses. Your tokens can be frozen in your own wallet.

921 of 4,183 ranked tokens measured

Example, USDC on Ethereum has blocklist functions: blacklist, isBlacklisted, unBlacklist.

A switch can stop your tokens. A key can rewrite them.

Some household names answer to one key.

The upgrade call is the proof. On Ethereum I replayed it at a pinned block: from the one wallet that holds the key it succeeds, from anyone else it reverts. USDC, PYUSD, cbBTC and BlackRock’s BUIDL all behave this way.

About four in ten of the top tokens can have their code replaced: 1,682 of the 4,041 we could read. For 314, a single wallet key can do it, with no multisig and no timelock in the way. For 875 more it takes a multisig, still with no timelock, so there is no delay and no warning before a change. Tokenized stocks and funds are a big part of it: 507 of the 510 can be upgraded.

What breaks Whoever holds the key can change what the token does for every holder at once. On-chain you can see which account holds the key, not how it is kept.

Part two: brand-new tokens

Now the newest tokens.

Those are the biggest, best-known tokens on six chains. The newest tokens get far less scrutiny, so I went looking at them next.

Buy it, wait an hour, try to sell.

Anyone can launch a token in minutes, and it can look fine on day one. So I took brand-new Ethereum tokens, found each one’s first trading pool, and waited about an hour (300 blocks). Then I simulated a test buy of 0.01 ETH and a sale in the next block. Nothing was ever sent on-chain: every test is replayed against saved chain state.

27,090 tokens that got a pool went through this, sampled by the month they were created.

What breaks A token you can buy may be one you cannot sell. Here that means the sale fails, or a tax of 10% or more takes the proceeds.

74.0%

of new tokens that launched with real liquidity in 2026 so far were a trap, or had already been emptied, within the hour. About three in four.

  1. A token launcheson Ethereum
  2. Its first pool gets liquiditytime zero
  3. Wait about an hour300 blocks
  4. Simulate a buy0.01 ETH
  5. Then try to sellin the next block
  • Sells normallythe sale goes through
  • A trapthe sale fails, or is taxed 10% or more
  • Nothing to sell intothe pool is already drained

That is the headline. It breaks into two stories, and the first one is good news.

The good news: far fewer traps.

Take the new tokens that still had real liquidity an hour in, at least 0.01 ETH in the pool. Of those created in 2024, 23.2% blocked the sale or taxed it 10% or more. In 2025 it was 7.7%. In 2026 so far it is 8.7%.

The peak was 2021, when 51.3% were traps.

That looks like progress. It is only half the picture.

The twist: the trap moved from “can’t sell” to “nothing left”.

Those shares only count tokens whose pool still had liquidity an hour in. For the rest there is nothing to sell into. Among all new tokens with a pool, the share already drained below 0.01 ETH went from 40.4% for 2024 launches to 55.6% in 2025 and 72.6% in 2026 so far.

In estimated counts, sale-blocking or heavily taxed tokens fell from about 13,205 among 2024 launches to about 1,868 so far in 2026. Drained pools went the other way, from about 41,743 among 2024 launches to 72,555 so far in 2026.

Put the two together. Of the tokens that started with real liquidity, the share that were a trap or emptied within the hour rose from 55.4% to 60.2% to 74.0%.

What breaks A falling trap rate hides the bigger risk: the pool you wanted to sell into is gone. This describes liquidity, not who removed it.

Some of the traps do not show up until later.

Some wait before they turn.

A token that sells normally at launch can change its mind. Among new tokens that looked normal at launch and kept their main pool (Uniswap V1 or V2), 19 of 110 sampled in 2026 so far were later restricted or taxed. That compares with 7 of 438 in 2024 and 7 of 303 in 2025. The samples are small, but the jump is big: about one in six, up from about one in sixty.

I read 24 of these cases by hand. They were fees raised to confiscatory levels, restrictions imposed from outside, and code installed at a fee wallet that used to be empty. In 9 of them that code was an EIP-7702 delegation, an Ethereum feature that lets an ordinary wallet run code.

What breaks A clean test at launch says nothing about next week. A token can be fine when you buy and a trap when you want out.

One last thing: my own measuring almost fooled me.

The measurement that almost fooled me.

Counting drained pools needs a line: a pool counts as live only above 0.01 ETH. My first version used a tiny line, and it showed a strange blip. On 2025-12-27, at Ethereum block 24,106,378, Uniswap V2 switched on its protocol fee. After that, when a provider pulled out of a pool, the protocol could be left holding a sliver of shares, and a small balance stayed behind.

That leftover could sit just above my tiny line, so a drained pool looked alive again. The balance was real, but it was only the protocol’s sliver plus the small amount every V2 pool locks away forever. The provider had left, and nothing had come back. I reproduced the fee formula on 10 saved receipts to be sure, then moved the line to 0.01 ETH and applied it the same way on every venue.

What breaks A line set too low counts a drained pool as alive, and new launches look healthier than they are.

Provider adds liquidity
Provider pulls out
old tiny linenew line, 0.01 ETH

Illustration, not to scale. The sliver is the protocol’s share from the V2 fee. It sits above the old line, so a drained pool read as live.

So how do I know the other checks are not fooling me too?

How I checked my own checks.

A simulator can be wrong, so I tested it against known answers. On a golden set of tokens whose behaviour is already documented, the probes matched 107 of the 114 expected results.

For launches, an independent harness replayed 376 launch states blind, freezing its verdicts before it saw my labels. 335 of 341 states above the liquidity floor gave a clear sellable-or-not answer, and the two disagreed on 4 of them.

It is a sample, so it cannot catch everything. Tests I could not replay this way rest on the simulator alone.

The ERC-20 label tells you very little.

If you build

Check balances before and after instead of trusting return values, test the deployment you will use rather than the ticker, and plan for pauses and freezes.

If you hold

Someone else may hold the switch.

If you buy new tokens

Of new tokens that launched with liquidity in 2026 so far, about three in four were a trap or empty within the hour. Try a small sale first.

How it was measured

The biggest tokens

  • Tested set: the top CoinGecko rank bands on each chain plus 542 extras, 4,740 deployments in all. Rates use the 4,198 ranked deployments; extras are shown separately. Only rank bands are published, never market data.
  • Every test is a read-only call or a local simulation against archive state; nothing is broadcast. Each cell keeps the raw request and response pointer, block, retrieval time and a sha256 of the saved response.
  • “Yes” answers the column’s question. Capability columns record what the code exposes; how or whether anyone uses it is outside what calls can show.
  • “Could not test” always carries a reason (no balance slot, transfers blocked, timeouts). It counts as neither yes nor no.
  • An upgrade path that ends at an externally owned account describes the on-chain account type. How that key is held (a person, MPC, a hardware module) is invisible on-chain.
  • Tornado Cash router rejections can come from a stale or independent policy list. The tested router is the one OFAC delisted on 2025-03-21.
  • 510 ranked deployments are tokenized stocks and funds, found by issuer name or listing. They lift the upgrade and blocklist shares, so the catalogue shows each rate with and without them.
  • Named issuers appear only next to a reproduced on-chain check, with the deployment and block stated.

The new launches

  • A probability sample of new Ethereum tokens by creation month; each token’s earliest pool with liquidity.
  • The test buy is 0.01 ETH, simulated 300 blocks after first liquidity, with the sale in the following block.
  • A pool counts as live when its real quote liquidity at that moment is at least 0.01 ETH, on every venue (V1/V2, V3, V4).
  • A trap means the sale fails or the tax is 10% or more. “Could not buy”, unresolved routes and below-floor pools are reported as their own categories.
  • Brackets are approximate 95% sampling intervals. They exclude classification error.
  • Any rate resting on an effective sample below 30 is withheld and shown as “Not reported”.
  • Drained pools are a description of liquidity, with no attribution to whoever withdrew it.
